findings.claim: gsm defined as "the standard measure of paper weight and thickness used across the industry"
findings.truth: Grammage (gsm) measures mass per square metre only. Thickness is measured in microns, as the same lesson states two sentences later and as its own flashcard answer requires.
findings.evidence: spec, Materials section 8: "The use of grammage i.e. grams per square metre (gsm) to measure weight of paper" and "The use of microns to measure thickness of card"

findings.claim: glossary entry "grammage (gsm)" repeats "weight and thickness"
findings.truth: Same error as F1 in the glossary the student revises from.
findings.evidence: spec, Materials section 8

findings.claim: "examiners reward precision"
findings.truth: A fabricated statement about examiner behaviour. The advice itself is sound; the appeal to examiners is invented.
findings.evidence: no such statement in the spec; house rule bans fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: "for the 12-mark Q6, answer ONE material area in depth - attempting more than one means only the first is marked"
findings.truth: The spec gives no question numbering and no per-question mark totals. It states only: written examination 2 hours, 50% of the qualification, 100 marks, a mix of short answer, structured and extended writing questions, plus in-depth knowledge in relation to at least one named material area. The rule that only the first attempt is marked is invented.
findings.evidence: spec lines 115-121 (Summary of Assessment) and 411-426 (2 hours, 100 marks, calculators allowed); spec p.15 in-depth list

findings.claim: "Q6 Strategy" heading, "The 12-mark extended response question", "A strong Q6 paragraph"
findings.truth: Same as F4: a board question code and a mark total the spec does not give. Replaced with house vocabulary ("in-depth", "extended writing question").
findings.evidence: spec lines 115-121 and 411-426; house rule bans board question codes

findings.claim: "Card and board start at roughly 200 gsm"
findings.truth: The paper/board threshold is a convention, not a standard. GCSE texts commonly teach 200 gsm; other sources place it near 170 gsm or 250 gsm (ISO 536). The lesson is internally consistent, so no edit.
findings.evidence: spec sets no threshold; convention varies by source

findings.claim: timber is "the most popular choice for the in-depth extended response question in the written exam"
findings.truth: No published entry data supports this. Softened to "a common choice".
findings.evidence: no source; spec silent on candidate choices

findings.claim: "the most popular choice for Question 6, and the exam mark scheme rewards depth rather than breadth"
findings.truth: Invented question number plus an invented mark-scheme claim.
findings.evidence: spec gives no question numbering; house rule bans mark-scheme quotation

findings.claim: "For 6-mark and 12-mark questions..." and "For Q6 on metals..."
findings.truth: Per-question mark totals and question codes are not in the spec.
findings.evidence: spec lines 115-121 and 411-426

findings.claim: "Examiner data shows that very few students choose polymers as their Q6 material"
findings.truth: Fabricated examiner data. No entry breakdown by material area is published.
findings.evidence: no source

findings.claim: collapsible heading "Avoiding Shallow Q6 Answers"
findings.truth: Board question code; replaced with house vocabulary.
findings.evidence: house rule bans board question codes

findings.claim: "For 12-mark Q6 responses..."; "Examiners flag that choosing polymers for Q6 is actually a chance to stand out - most students pick timber, so a well-prepared polymer answer impresses at the top band"; "answer only ONE Q6 in the exam"
findings.truth: Fabricated examiner claim plus unsupported mark total and question code. The one true part (answer one material area in depth) is kept.
findings.evidence: spec p.15 in-depth list; spec lines 115-121

findings.claim: property table lists "cotton (wet)" as a LOW strength example
findings.truth: Cotton is one of the few fibres that is stronger wet than dry (wet tenacity about 105-120% of dry). The fibre that loses strength badly when wet is viscose rayon. Teaching the reverse is a classic misconception and would cost marks in a fibre-comparison question.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Rayon: "The durability and appearance retention of regular viscose rayons are low, especially when wet"; standard textile science on cotton wet tenacity; the same lesson already says linen is "stronger than cotton when wet", a comparison, not a weakness

findings.claim: "For the 12-mark Q6 on fibres and textiles..."
findings.truth: Mark total and question code not supported by the spec.
findings.evidence: spec lines 115-121 and 411-426

findings.claim: "Tactel - a branded form of nylon microfibre developed by Invista"
findings.truth: Tactel was developed by ICI in the 1980s; the brand passed to DuPont and then to Invista, which owns it now. Not mark-affecting.
findings.evidence: brand ownership history

findings.claim: "The specification names two branded fibres explicitly: Tactel ... Tencel"
findings.truth: The spec also names Lycra under synthetic fibres. Tactel and Tencel are the two named microfibres. The claim is loose rather than wrong in substance.
findings.evidence: spec, Materials section 12: "Synthetic: polyester, polypropylene, nylon, acrylic, elastane, lycra, aramid fibres" and "Microfibres - Tactel, Tencel (Lyocell)"

findings.claim: flashcard [11]: "2/1 means the weft passes over 2 warp threads then under 1" (about denim)
findings.truth: Denim is a warp-faced twill: the weft passes UNDER two or more warp threads, so the indigo-dyed warp floats on the face. The flashcard inverts the structure, which also contradicts the lesson's own "indigo-dyed warp" note and the reason jeans wear white on the inside.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Denim: "the weft passes under two or more warp threads"

findings.claim: satin weave "Used in eveningwear, linings, bedding and parachute fabric"
findings.truth: Parachute canopies are ripstop plain weave (nylon today, silk historically), not satin. The other three uses are right.
findings.evidence: parachute canopy fabric construction; the same unit's L5 correctly gives silk as the historic parachute fibre, not satin as the weave

findings.claim: "this is a distinct examiner-friendly fact" and "For 12-mark Q6 questions on fibres and textiles..."
findings.truth: Fabricated examiner claim plus unsupported mark total and question code.
findings.evidence: spec lines 115-121 and 411-426

findings.claim: Q2 "Name the thermoforming polymer that has a 'living hinge' property." is banded 2 marks, and the key awards "Polypropylene (PP) [2 marks]" with no partial-credit route. Lesson 2 Q2 has the same 2-mark "Name" shape but does give a 1-mark fallback.
findings.truth: Two options. (a) Re-band Lesson 4 Q2 as "1 mark - Name" with "Polypropylene (PP) [1 mark]", matching every other single-term recall question in the unit. (b) Keep 2 marks and add a partial-credit route, as Lesson 2 Q2 does. A one-word answer worth 2 marks with no way to score 1 teaches the wrong sense of how much to write.
findings.evidence: internal comparison across the unit's practice sets; spec gives no per-question mark totals
findings.ruling: Leave: single-term 2-mark tariff to the relabel queue.

findings.claim: "denim (2/1 twill with indigo-dyed warp)"
findings.truth: Most denim is a 3/1 warp-faced twill; 2/1 exists in lighter denims. Wikipedia's "two or more warp threads" covers both, so the figure stands. Left unedited.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Denim

summary: Technical content across the six lessons is strong: timber categorisation, metal carbon percentages, polymer categories and named examples, fibre sources and weave/knit structures all check out against the spec, and all 30 knowledge-check keys are correct. The real damage is exam framing - five of six lessons assert a numbered 12-mark question and quote invented examiner or mark-scheme behaviour, none of which the spec supports. Two technical fixes: cotton listed as a low-strength-when-wet fibre (it is stronger wet; viscose is the weak one) and a flashcard that inverts denim's warp-faced twill.
